findings.title: v3 downgrade uses a non-deterministic correlated subquery; silently drops run history
findings.description: downgrade() runs `UPDATE tasks SET result_json = (SELECT result_json FROM task_results WHERE task_results.task_id = tasks.id)`. The subquery is a scalar context but returns one row per task_results entry; on SQLite the multi-row scalar subquery silently picks an arbitrary row instead of erroring (on SQLite >= 3.39 it raises 'subquery must return only one row'). For a task with N>=2 runs the downgrade 'succeeds' but only one run's payload survives — silently losing (N-1)/N of the run history. AC-7.2's byte-identical round-trip is violated whenever a task has been run more than once.
findings.code_snippet:
bind.execute(
    sa.text(
        "UPDATE tasks SET result_json = ("
        "SELECT result_json FROM task_results "
        "WHERE task_results.task_id = tasks.id"
        ")"
    )
)
findings.reasoning: v3_split_results.py:92-100 emits an UPDATE with a scalar-context subquery. When task_results has multiple rows for the same task_id (the v3 multi-run schema's whole point), the subquery returns >1 row. SQLite's documented behavior for multi-row scalar subqueries is undefined for pre-3.39 (silent arbitrary pick) and a hard error for 3.39+. The downgrade 'succeeds' with one row of three restored — data loss. Repro: 3 runs inserted, downgrade runs, readback returns '{"run": 0}' instead of '{"run": 2}' (the latest).
findings.suggested_fix: Pick a deterministic single row: ORDER BY started_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1 inside the subquery, matching task_repo.list_runs's ordering.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: v3_split_results.py:92-100 emits the broken correlated subquery; executed repro inserted 3 task_results rows, ran alembic downgrade -1, read tasks.result_json — got '{"run": 0}' (silent arbitrary pick) instead of '{"run": 2}' (latest). Refuter could not find a guard, fallback, or LIMIT that limits the subquery to a single row. The pre-fix test_ac_7_2 only inserts one row per task, so the multi-run case was never covered.

findings.title: _AdmissionGate never releases slots — submit() permanently refuses after cap lifetime submissions
findings.description: _AdmissionGate decrements _remaining on every admission and has no release path, so TASKQ_MAX_CONCURRENT is a process-lifetime budget rather than a concurrency limit. Once cap submissions have EVER completed, every later submit() returns final_state='queued' without spawning a subprocess and without ever being retried — a permanent, silent execution outage.
findings.reasoning: runner.py:129-132 mutates _remaining downward only; the whole module contains no increment. _get_gate (runner.py:143-149) only rebuilds the gate when the configured cap CHANGES, so the counter is never reset in a stable deployment. Empirical repro with TASKQ_MAX_CONCURRENT=2 and four SEQUENTIAL submits (each awaited to completion before the next): states == ['done','done','queued','queued'] — submissions 3 and 4 were refused with nothing in flight.
findings.suggested_fix: Add _AdmissionGate.release() and call it from submit()'s finally block.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: runner.py:130 is the only write to _remaining; runner.py:147 rebuilds the gate only on cap change. Refuter could not cite any release/reset path. Executed repro output: ['done','done','queued','queued'].

findings.title: Spawn failure (missing binary) escapes the runner and strands the task in 'running'
findings.description: _collect_outcome only catches asyncio.TimeoutError. asyncio.create_subprocess_exec raises FileNotFoundError/PermissionError when the resolved binary does not exist or is not executable; that OSError propagates out of _run_and_persist BEFORE record_result/update_status run, so no task_results row is written and the task row stays at state='running' forever. Via POST /v1/tasks/{id}/run the exception dies inside the fire-and-forget asyncio task, so the client never learns.
findings.reasoning: execute_command (runner.py:191) calls create_subprocess_exec with argv[0] from shlex.split; a nonexistent path raises FileNotFoundError, which is an OSError, not TimeoutError. _run_and_persist (runner.py:276-285) writes the result row only AFTER the await returns, so the raise skips both persistence calls. Executed repro: run_task on command '/nonexistent/binary arg' raised FileNotFoundError; task status after == 'running'; task_results rows == 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Catch (OSError, ValueError) in _collect_outcome and map to STATE_FAILED with the OS error in stderr_tail.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: runner.py:238 catches only asyncio.TimeoutError; runner.py:276 is unreachable on the raise. Executed repro printed 'FileNotFoundError ... status: running, run rows: 0'.

findings.title: /v1/metrics reports a frozen rate_limit_denials — always the import-time value (0)
findings.description: api.health binds rate_limit_denials to the VALUE of ratelimit_service.denial_count at import time. ratelimit.record_denial() rebinds the service module's global int, which cannot mutate the already-copied binding in api.health, so the metrics_route body always returned 0 no matter how many 429s were served. FR-09's rate_limit_denials observability field was inert.
findings.reasoning: health.py:52 copies an immutable int at import; ratelimit.py:29-32 does 'global denial_count; denial_count += 1' which rebinds only ratelimit.denial_count. health.py:231 returned the stale copy. Executed repro after two record_denial() calls: ratelimit.denial_count == 2 while health.rate_limit_denials == 0 and metrics_route()['rate_limit_denials'] == 0.
findings.suggested_fix: Read ratelimit_service.denial_count inside metrics_route instead of the module-level copy.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: health.py:52 + ratelimit.py:31 rebinding semantics; executed repro shows 2 vs 0.

findings.title: T-05 mitigation: 3-substring denylist lets absolute paths outside /Users leak in the 500 detail
findings.description: _sanitize_detail masks a 500 detail only when the raw exception message contains 'Traceback', 'SQL' or '/Users'. Any unhandled exception whose message embeds a deployment path (/home/..., /opt/..., /var/...) — the normal case on a Linux container, the actual deployment target — is echoed verbatim into the problem+json body.
findings.reasoning: app.py:64 hardcodes a macOS-only home prefix. app.py:227 feeds str(exc) straight into _make_500_body. Executed: _sanitize_detail("[Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/home/deploy/secrets/taskq.db'") returns the string UNCHANGED. Severity is medium rather than high because reaching it requires an unhandled exception on an authenticated /v1 route; every currently-known route path funnels through Problem handlers.
findings.suggested_fix: Allowlist instead: emit a constant 'Internal server error.' for every 500 and keep the raw message only in the log.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: app.py:64 + app.py:85-88; executed sanitizer returned the path unchanged.
findings.attack_vector: T-05 information_disclosure — unhandled exception leaks stack trace / SQL / file paths via detail field
findings.attempted_exploit: Drive _sanitize_detail with a Linux-style absolute path in the exception message (FileNotFoundError on /home/deploy/secrets/taskq.db).

findings.title: Production auth branches on a test stub's __name__ (test-shaped backdoor)
findings.description: _is_wrong_key_stub_active inspects key_repo.get_active_by_hash.__name__ == '_stub_active' and changes resolve_api_key's return value accordingly. Production behaviour is coupled to a test double's identifier: anything that monkeypatches or wraps get_active_by_hash with a function of that name flips the branch.
findings.reasoning: auth.py:60 reads the callable's name at request time; auth.py:92-99 selects NOT_FOUND vs None from it. Both values are treated identically as 401 by deps.py:87, so there is no privilege-escalation path — hence medium, not high. The defect is that test scaffolding is compiled into the production decision.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete _is_wrong_key_stub_active; always return NOT_FOUND on the no-row path and adjust the FR-03 test.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: auth.py:60 verbatim; refuter established the 401 outcome is identical either way (deps.py:87), which caps severity at medium.

findings.title: T-02 mitigation: rate limiting is fail-open and never applies before authentication
findings.description: _enforce_rate_limit wraps ratelimit.check in a bare 'except Exception: return', admitting the request whenever the bucket engine errors. It is also only invoked AFTER _resolve_or_raise succeeds, so an unauthenticated flood of bad X-API-Key values is never throttled while each attempt still performs a get_active_by_hash SELECT against the pool.
findings.code_snippet:
try:
    allowed, retry_after = ratelimit.check(key_id)
except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
    return
findings.reasoning: deps.py:51-56 swallows every bucket failure and admits; deps.py:149-153 places _enforce_rate_limit strictly after _resolve_or_raise. The declared T-02 threat is 'excessive request volume exhausts DB connections' — the unauthenticated arm of that volume bypasses the bucket entirely, and each 401 attempt opens a session via key_repo.get_active_by_hash (key_repo.py:70). The token bucket itself (rate_repo.withdraw) is correct for authenticated callers, so this is a coverage gap, not a broken bucket.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail closed (429) on bucket errors, and apply a coarse per-IP bucket before key resolution.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmer: deps.py:53 bare except + deps.py:149-153 ordering; key_repo.py:70 opens a session_scope per unauthenticated attempt.
findings.attack_vector: T-02 denial_of_service — excessive request volume exhausts DB connections or async slots
findings.attempted_exploit: Flood /v1/tasks with invalid X-API-Key headers; each request reaches key_repo.get_active_by_hash without ever charging a bucket, and any bucket-engine error admits authenticated floods too.

findings.title: list_tasks_endpoint accepts a negative limit
findings.description: Only the upper bound (>200) is checked; limit=-5 reaches list_paginated, which issues LIMIT -4. On SQLite a negative LIMIT means 'no limit', so the guard's intent (bounded page size) is defeated on a negative input.
findings.reasoning: tasks.py:109 tests only the upper bound; task_repo.py:129 applies .limit(limit + 1) unconditionally. Low severity: the page-size DoS needs a negative value AND SQLite's negative-LIMIT semantics, and each row is still eagerly loaded once (no N+1).
findings.suggested_fix: Reject effective_limit < 1 with the same 422 problem.

findings.title: T-03 (spoofing) — declared mitigation verified effective
findings.description: Threat-model seed T-03: forged or revoked X-API-Key; replay attempts. The declared mitigation was exercised against the attack, not merely inspected for defensive-looking code.
findings.reasoning: auth.py:86-87 hashes the candidate and looks it up; key_repo.py:74 filters revoked_at IS NOT NULL out of the query, so a revoked key yields row=None -> 401 at deps.py:87-93. findings.title: T-07 (denial_of_service) — declared mitigation verified effective
findings.description: Threat-model seed T-07: long-running command exhausts the host process table or blocks shutdown. The declared mitigation was exercised against the attack, not merely inspected for defensive-looking code.
findings.reasoning: Every production entry point supplies a budget: _run_and_persist (runner.py:272-274) falls back to TASKQ_TASK_TIMEOUT, and runner.py:198 wraps communicate() in asyncio.wait_for. Both the TimeoutError path (runner.py:205-207) and the CancelledError path (runner.py:214-216) do proc.kill() then await proc.wait(), so the child is reaped rather than orphaned; drain() (runner.py:390-411) bounds the shutdown wait and marks stragglers interrupted.
